mcqs: Cu⁺ is [Ar]3d¹⁰: all electrons are paired.
Ni²⁺ (3d⁸), Cr³⁺ (3d³) and Mn²⁺ (3d⁵) have unpaired electrons and are paramagnetic. So Cu⁺ is diamagnetic.
Potassium ferrocyanide K₄[Fe(CN)₆] contains the complex ion [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, which keeps its identity in solution.
Cu²⁺ with four chloride ligands forms [CuCl₄]²⁻, which is (distorted) tetrahedral.
Let the oxidation state of Cr be x: x + 2(−2) + 2(−1) = 0.
Be²⁺ has no d orbitals; it uses sp³ hybrid orbitals for four F⁻ ligands.
A typical transition element has an incompletely filled d subshell in the atom or a common ion.
Zn and Cd have completely filled d¹⁰ subshells and Ra is an s-block element; cobalt (3d⁷4s²) is a typical transition element.
Paramagnetism arises from unpaired electrons, each with an uncompensated spin magnetic moment.
It depends on the number of unpaired electrons.
Ligands donate a lone pair of electrons to the central metal ion to form coordinate bonds.
Fe, Co and Ni are the ferromagnetic metals.
Six CN⁻ ligands are each bonded to Fe through one donor atom.
A bidentate ligand bonds through two donor atoms.
Oxalate C₂O₄²⁻ binds through two oxygen atoms; H₂O, NH₃ and CO are monodentate.
In [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ the ligands split the 3d orbitals.
Absorption of red-orange light promotes an electron from a lower to a higher d orbital (d–d transition), so the solution looks blue.
It accepts electrons easily, so potassium dichromate is a strong oxidising agent.
German silver is an alloy of copper, zinc and nickel (it contains no silver).
In naming coordination compounds, anionic ligands end in -o (chlorido, cyanido), but neutral ligands keep their names (e.g. ethylenediamine).
Common exceptions are aqua (H₂O), ammine (NH₃), carbonyl (CO) and nitrosyl (NO).
shortQuestions: Cu⁺: [Ar]3d¹⁰ — all ten d electrons are paired, so there is no net magnetic moment and it is diamagnetic.
Cu²⁺: [Ar]3d⁹ — one unpaired electron gives a magnetic moment, so it is paramagnetic.
Sc [Ar]3d¹4s², Ti [Ar]3d²4s², V [Ar]3d³4s², Cr [Ar]3d⁵4s¹, Mn [Ar]3d⁵4s².
Fe [Ar]3d⁶4s², Co [Ar]3d⁷4s², Ni [Ar]3d⁸4s², Cu [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹, Zn [Ar]3d¹⁰4s².
Transition metals show variable oxidation states, so they can form unstable intermediate compounds and then regenerate (e.g. Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺).
They have vacant d orbitals and large surface areas, so reactant molecules are adsorbed and their bonds weakened.
Both provide an alternative reaction path of lower activation energy, so they act as catalysts.
Transition metal ions are small and highly charged (high charge density), so they strongly attract ligands.
They have vacant (n−1)d, ns and np orbitals of suitable energy that can accept lone pairs from ligands, forming coordinate bonds and complex ions.
The (n−1)d and ns orbitals have very similar energies.
So electrons from both the 4s and the 3d subshells can be lost or shared in different numbers, giving several oxidation states (e.g. Mn shows +2 to +7).
Scandium forms compounds only in the +3 state; Sc³⁺ has the configuration [Ar] with no 3d electrons.
With no d electrons there can be no d–d transitions, so its compounds absorb no visible light and are colourless; with no unpaired electrons they are diamagnetic.
Transition elements have partly filled d subshells; s- and p-block elements do not.
Transition elements show variable oxidation states, form coloured and paramagnetic compounds, form many complexes, act as catalysts and are hard, dense metals with high melting points and alloys.
s-block elements show fixed oxidation states (+1, +2) and mostly colourless, diamagnetic compounds; p-block elements include non-metals and form mainly covalent compounds.
H₂O is a neutral ligand, so the charge of the complex equals the charge of Cr.
x + 6(0) = +3, so chromium is in the +3 oxidation state.
In the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃) iron adsorbs N₂ and H₂ on its surface and weakens their bonds — a reducing environment in which iron stays metallic.

In the contact process the catalyst must transfer oxygen to SO₂ by changing oxidation state reversibly (V₂O₅ ⇌ V₂O₄). In the oxidising, acidic SO₂/SO₃ atmosphere iron would be oxidised and converted into iron sulphate (catalyst poisoned), so V₂O₅ (or Pt) is used instead.
Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰: the d subshell is full, so no d–d transition is possible; no visible light is absorbed and its salts are white.
Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹: an electron can be promoted between split d orbitals by absorbing visible (red-orange) light, so its salts are coloured (blue).
longQuestions: (a) Electronic structures of 3d elements: Sc [Ar]3d¹4s², Ti 3d²4s², V 3d³4s², Cr 3d⁵4s¹, Mn 3d⁵4s², Fe 3d⁶4s², Co 3d⁷4s², Ni 3d⁸4s², Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹, Zn 3d¹⁰4s².
(b) By the Aufbau principle chromium would be 3d⁴4s² and copper 3d⁹4s². Instead Cr is 3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is 3d¹⁰4s¹.
The 3d and 4s energies are very close, and a half-filled (d⁵) or completely filled (d¹⁰) subshell has extra stability (symmetrical distribution and greater exchange energy).
So one 4s electron moves into the 3d subshell, giving the more stable half-filled or filled arrangement.

(a) Origin of colour: in a complex the ligands split the five d orbitals into two sets of different energy (crystal-field splitting Δ). An electron in a lower d orbital absorbs a photon of visible light whose energy equals Δ and jumps to a higher d orbital (d–d transition). The complementary colour of the absorbed light is seen, e.g. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs orange-red and looks blue. The colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligands. Ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ are colourless.

(b) General characteristics of transition elements: metals with high melting and boiling points, hardness and density; variable oxidation states; coloured ions; paramagnetism; formation of complexes; catalytic activity; formation of interstitial compounds and alloys.

(c) Vanadium: V₂O₅ catalyses the contact process, 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃, by changing oxidation state: V₂O₅ + SO₂ → V₂O₄ + SO₃, then V₂O₄ + ½O₂ → V₂O₅. Iron: finely divided iron (promoted with K₂O and Al₂O₃) catalyses the Haber process N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ by adsorbing the gases on its surface; Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ ions also catalyse the reaction between I⁻ and S₂O₈²⁻ by switching oxidation state.

IUPAC rules: (1) Name the cation first, then the anion. (2) Within the complex, name the ligands first in alphabetical order, then the metal. (3) Number of ligands: di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa- (bis-, tris- for complicated ligands).
(4) Anionic ligands end in -o: chlorido (Cl⁻), cyanido (CN⁻), hydroxido (OH⁻), oxalato (C₂O₄²⁻). Neutral ligands keep their names, except aqua (H₂O), ammine (NH₃), carbonyl (CO), nitrosyl (NO).
(5) The oxidation state of the metal is given in Roman numerals in brackets. (6) If the complex is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate (ferrate, cuprate, argentate, aurate).

Examples: [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ — tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate; K₄[Fe(CN)₆] — potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II); [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ — pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride; [Ni(CO)₄] — tetracarbonylnickel(0); K₂[PtCl₆] — potassium hexachloridoplatinate(IV).

(a) Potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄, is a strong oxidising agent. Cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄ oxidises alkenes to diols (Baeyer's test — the purple colour disappears and brown MnO₂ forms): CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + [O] → HOCH₂–CH₂OH.

Hot acidified KMnO₄ cleaves alkenes (e.g. to carboxylic acids or ketones), oxidises primary alcohols to carboxylic acids (RCH₂OH + 2[O] → RCOOH + H₂O), aldehydes to acids, and side chains of benzene rings to benzoic acid: C₆H₅CH₃ + 3[O] → C₆H₅COOH + H₂O. In acid, MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.

(b) An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals (or a metal with a non-metal), e.g. brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), steel (Fe + C), German silver (Cu + Zn + Ni), stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni).

Properties different from the component metals: alloys are usually harder and stronger (different-sized atoms stop the layers sliding), have lower melting points, better resistance to corrosion, and lower electrical and thermal conductivity; their colour may differ.

(a) Copper shows +1 and +2 oxidation states. Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) occurs in insoluble or solid compounds such as Cu₂O and CuCl; in water Cu⁺ disproportionates: 2Cu⁺ → Cu + Cu²⁺. Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) is the most common and stable state in aqueous solution, forming blue [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (CuSO₄, CuCl₂, Cu(NO₃)₂).
(b) With hydroxide ions: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → [Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂] + 2H₂O, a pale blue precipitate.
With ammonia: a little ammonia gives the same pale blue precipitate; with excess ammonia it dissolves to a deep blue solution: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4H₂O.
With carbonate ions: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → CuCO₃ + 6H₂O, a blue-green precipitate (basic copper carbonate).
activities: Observations: on heating, the deep blue crystals of CuSO₄·5H₂O gradually turn pale and finally become a white powder; water vapour is given off and may condense on the cooler parts of the container.
After heating, the blue colour disappears and white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate remains, because the water of crystallisation has been driven off.
The blue colour comes from Cu²⁺ ions surrounded by water molecules acting as ligands. These ligands split the 3d orbitals so that red-orange light is absorbed in d–d transitions.
When the water is removed, this ligand arrangement is lost; the anhydrous salt absorbs no visible light, so the colour disappears.
The colour change is caused by the loss of water ligands: in CuSO₄·5H₂O, [Cu(H₂O)₄]²⁺ units have a crystal-field splitting that matches visible light.
In anhydrous CuSO₄ the Cu²⁺ ion is surrounded by sulphate oxygens, which give a different splitting whose absorption lies outside the visible region, so the solid looks white.
On adding water, the white powder turns blue again and becomes warm (the reaction is exothermic).
CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s). This is used as a test for water.
Water molecules again coordinate to the Cu²⁺ ions as ligands, restoring the d-orbital splitting.
The d–d transitions absorb red-orange light once more, so the deep blue colour reappears.
